purpose: Editorial recommendation metadata and source provenance for the three representative writing articles. These fields are kept outside the strict Commons frontmatter schema.

articles.title: Let the Verb Do the Work
use_when: Modifiers repeat information already carried by a verb.
A broad verb and surrounding explanation conceal the intended action.
A revision uses more dramatic verbs without checking whether their meaning is accurate.
not_ideal_when: A modifier adds essential information about intention, duration, degree, or contrast.
A plain verb or ongoing construction serves the passage's focus and rhythm.
example_user_queries: My sentences have lots of adverbs and still feel vague.
How can I make actions easier to picture?
I keep adding very and really to everything.
When should I keep an adverb?
My edited prose sounds more dramatic than what actually happened.
Can I use said without making dialogue boring?
I want to shorten my wording without losing nuance.
Every verb in my story sounds as if it came from a thesaurus.
I cannot tell whether this modifier adds anything.
Is a simple verb sometimes better than a colorful one?

visual_decision.implementation: Connected prose follows a workshop-key exchange through alternative revisions, explaining each choice before drawing out its consequences. No table or separate graphic is used.

sources.author: Roy Peter Clark
sources.title: Fifty Writing Tools: Quick List
sources.inspected_material: Primary-source indexed excerpt of tools 3 and 5, distinguishing verb activation from adverbs that change meaning. Direct page retrieval returned HTTP 403.
sources.supports: The selective treatment of verb choice and meaningful adverbs.
sources.limits: No claim to have inspected the full Writing Tools book. No Stephen King passage is attributed or quoted.

articles.title: Show What Matters, Summarize the Rest
use_when: Routine intervals consume more space than consequential encounters.
Important emotions or changes are announced without an experience that makes them tangible.
Applying a blanket showing rule has produced excessive small actions and withheld context.
not_ideal_when: The purpose requires a concise record rather than a dramatized reconstruction.
The factual record does not support exact dialogue or attributed interior experience.
example_user_queries: My story describes every small action and moves too slowly.
I keep saying how characters feel instead of making it convincing.
Which moments in my story deserve a full scene?
Can I summarize the months between important events?
I followed show don't tell and now my draft is twice as long.
The big conversation in my story is over before readers can care.
How can I move through routine events without making them dull?
My scene has lots of sensory details but nothing seems to happen.
When is directly explaining a relationship useful?
How do I write about a real conversation when I cannot remember the exact words?

visual_decision.implementation: Developed passages compare a compressed announcement, an expanded conversation, a compressed aftermath, and a cumulative summary. Narrative duration is explained in prose without a separate table.

sources.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
sources.title: Navigating the Ocean of Story, Session 1
sources.inspected_material: The answer to Paige's question on showing and telling, preserved on the author's site; originally posted 10 August 2015.
sources.supports: Telling can remain vivid and moving; the maxim should not become a blanket ban on narration.
sources.limits: The merged pattern formulation and comparisons of narrative attention are original synthesis. No passage-level claim about Steering the Craft, Writing Fiction, or Draft No. 4 is made.

articles.title: Set Up and Pay Off
use_when: A late solution depends on an object or ability that has not been established.
An early detail receives conspicuous attention but no later significance.
An emotional return is understandable to the writer but not prepared for the reader.
not_ideal_when: An incidental detail serves atmosphere without creating an expectation of later use.
An imposed setup would distort the factual record or make preparation excessively obvious.
example_user_queries: The solution at the end of my story feels too convenient.
How can I introduce a clue without making it obvious?
My character suddenly has a skill the reader has never seen.
Do I need a twist for an ending to be satisfying?
An early detail in my story seems to promise something that never happens.
I want a small farewell gesture to carry more meaning.
How much preparation does a late reveal need?
Readers can guess the ending and I am unsure whether that is a problem.
My callback repeats an object but does not seem to matter.
How can an essay return to its opening with a new understanding?

visual_decision.implementation: A complete emotional-return example establishes invitation, refusal, and later acceptance. Separate practical and essay examples explain the same relationship in context. No dependency table is needed.

sources.author: Brandon Sanderson's official site
sources.title: Brandon Sanderson's 2025 Guide to Plot (Lecture #2)
sources.inspected_material: The official notes' sections on promise, progress, and payoff, including expectations and the possibility of effective payoffs without a twist.
sources.supports: A related framework connecting established expectations, development, and eventual payoff.
sources.limits: The notes are not treated as a transcript personally written by Sanderson or an origin claim for setup and payoff. The dependency analysis and examples are original. The proposed Saunders and Burroway book passages remain unverified leads.
